entries.name: Partial Information Decomposition
entries.senseHere: A method that splits the total information two or more sources give about a target into separate pieces: information both sources share redundantly, information each gives uniquely, and information only visible when their patterns are combined (synergy). The article uses this breakdown to study how neurons combine inputs rather than just transmit them.

entries.name: rich club
entries.senseHere: A set of the most highly and densely interconnected neurons in a network, connected to each other far more than chance would predict. The article finds these neurons carry a disproportionate share of all synergistic computation in cortical circuits.

entries.name: mutual information
entries.senseHere: A measure of how much knowing the state of one neuron reduces uncertainty about the state of another, treated in the article as a kind of nonlinear correlation between two patterns of activity with no sense of direction or time.

entries.name: transfer entropy
entries.senseHere: A directional measure of how much a neuron's past activity reduces uncertainty about another neuron's future activity, beyond what that second neuron's own past already explains. The article uses it to build networks showing the flow, not just the correlation, of activity between neurons.

entries.name: functional connectivity
entries.senseHere: A description of which neurons' activity is statistically dependent on which others, measured without regard to the direction or timing of any causal influence; the article equates this with what mutual information captures.

entries.name: effective connectivity
entries.senseHere: A description of which neurons actually appear to send information forward in time to which others, as opposed to merely being correlated; the article equates this with what transfer entropy captures.

entries.name: synergy
entries.senseHere: The portion of information about a neuron's future activity that can only be learned by observing two or more source neurons together, not from any one of them alone. The article treats high synergy as a sign that a neuron is genuinely combining or computing on its inputs rather than just adding them up.

entries.name: redundancy
entries.senseHere: Information about a target neuron that could be learned equally well from either of two source neurons on its own, so it gets double-counted if you simply add up what each source tells you.

entries.name: unique information
entries.senseHere: The part of what a source neuron tells you about a target that no other source neuron could tell you.

entries.name: redundancy function
entries.senseHere: A formula chosen to define exactly how much information counts as 'shared' between sources, which is needed before any of the other information pieces (unique, synergistic) can be calculated; the article notes there is no single agreed formula for this.

entries.name: computational triad
entries.senseHere: A unit of analysis consisting of two source neurons that both connect to one shared target neuron, used as the basic building block for applying PID across a whole recorded network.

entries.name: partial information lattice
entries.senseHere: A diagram that organizes every possible combination of source neurons into a hierarchy, used to calculate how much information is uniquely attributable to each combination once simpler combinations have been accounted for.

entries.name: Möbius inversion
entries.senseHere: A mathematical procedure applied to the partial information lattice that calculates each information piece by subtracting out everything already accounted for by simpler combinations of sources below it.

entries.name: organotypic cultures
entries.senseHere: Thin slices of living brain tissue grown in a dish that retain much of their original cell connectivity, used as the source of the multielectrode neural recordings analyzed in the article.

entries.name: connectivity motif
entries.senseHere: The pattern of wiring within a computational triad, classified as feedforward (source-to-target), feedback (target-back-to-source), or recurrent (between the two sources), used to test which wiring patterns boost synergy.

entries.name: Dedekind number
entries.senseHere: A rapidly growing count that gives the exact number of distinct information pieces in a PID lattice for a given number of source neurons, illustrating why decomposing more than a handful of sources quickly becomes computationally impossible.

entries.name: O-information
entries.senseHere: A simplified, faster-to-compute measure of whether a group of variables is on balance more redundant or more synergistic, used as a practical stand-in for full PID when the number of sources is too large for a complete decomposition.

entries.name: local PID
entries.senseHere: A version of PID applied to a single specific moment or configuration of activity rather than averaged over all possible states, allowing researchers to build a time-resolved trace of redundancy and synergy as they change moment to moment.

entries.name: integrated information decomposition
entries.senseHere: An extension of PID that decomposes information shared between two or more sources and two or more targets at once, rather than just one target, allowing analysis of how information flows over time between whole sets of variables.
